reference: Postpartum (if the newborn is Rh-positive) Administer within 72 hours of delivery ... RhoGAM (300 µg) (1500 IU) ... indicated for administration to Rh-negative women not previously sensitized to the Rho(D) factor ... Administer 20 µg of RhoGAM per mL of Rh-positive red blood cell exposure, rounding up to the next whole syringe.

question: A 58-year-old man (70 kg) presents to the ED with fever, headache, neck stiffness and confusion. LP is performed; CSF shows 4,200 WBC (92% neutrophils), glucose 18, protein 220, and Gram stain shows gram-positive diplococci. No antibiotics have yet been given. Neurology gives IV dexamethasone 10–20 min before the first dose of ceftriaxone + vancomycin. Which dexamethasone regimen is indicated?

reference: Dose: "0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours"; Duration: "2-4 days"; Timing: "10–20 min before, or at least concomitant with, the first dose of antimicrobial therapy."

question: A 44-year-old man has biopsy-proven anti-GBM disease diagnosed 3 d ago (crescents in 40% of glomeruli, no fibrosis); serum anti-GBM antibody strongly positive; creatinine 3.1 mg/dL with preserved urine output and no dialysis requirement; no pulmonary hemorrhage; no active bleeding or recent surgery. Oral cyclophosphamide and prednisolone have been started. Nephrology plans plasma exchange. Which schedule is indicated?

choices.C: Daily sessions continued until serum creatinine normalizes
choices.D: Daily sessions × 14 d, or until anti-GBM antibody is undetectable

reference: "Daily 40–60 mL/kg exchange for 5% human albumin solution" ... "Continue until antibody levels are fully suppressed, typically 14 days" ... "Monitor antibody levels regularly during and after cessation of treatment; PEX may require reinstatement if antibody levels rebound." Cyclophosphamide "2–3 mg/kg/day (ideal body weight; maximum 200 mg) orally for 2–3 months" and "Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg) orally."

question: A 58-year-old man presents 6 hr after sudden dyspnea and a syncopal episode. CTA confirms a saddle pulmonary embolism; BP is 76/44 after 1 L of crystalloid, HR 124, echo shows RV dilation with septal flattening, troponin elevated. No recent surgery, stroke, head trauma, intracranial disease, bleeding diathesis, or uncontrolled hypertension. IV unfractionated heparin has been started. Cardiology proposes systemic thrombolysis. Which regimen is indicated?

reference: "The recommended dose is 100 mg administered by IV infusion over 2 hours." Contraindications: "Active internal bleeding"; "Recent intracranial or intraspinal surgery or serious head trauma"; "Intracranial conditions that may increase the risk of bleeding"; "Bleeding diathesis"; "Current severe uncontrolled hypertension"; for PE also "History of recent stroke."

question: A 26-year-old Rh-negative woman at 10 wk gestation presents with vaginal bleeding that began 12 hr ago (threatened miscarriage; fetal cardiac activity present on ultrasound). Antibody screen is negative, so she is not already alloimmunized. She has not received anti-D immune globulin in this pregnancy. OB orders anti-D IG now. Which order is correct?

reference: "Actual or threatened termination of pregnancy (spontaneous or induced) up to and including 12 weeks gestation. Administer within 72 hours." ... administration "within 72 hours of suspected or proven exposure to Rh-positive red blood cells."

question: A 68-year-old woman collapses in the ED; the monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. High-quality CPR is in progress; she has received three defibrillation shocks and IV epinephrine, and VF persists. No antiarrhythmic has been given yet. The code team gives amiodarone as a rapid IV bolus. Which dose is indicated for this first antiarrhythmic dose?

reference: "initial IV/IO dose of 300 mg with a second IV/IO dose of 150 mg if required" — "Amiodarone or lidocaine may be considered for VF/pVT that is unresponsive to defibrillation" (Class IIb, LOE B-R).

question: A 34-year-old woman (45 kg) with bee-sting anaphylaxis (BP 78/48, bronchospasm, diffuse urticaria) receives IM epinephrine 0.3 mg mid-thigh, IV fluids, and H1/H2 blockers, with resolution of the hypotension and wheeze. Two hours into observation she reports a moderate headache and myalgias. She remains nauseated and is not tolerating oral intake. No liver disease; no acetaminophen in the preceding 24 hr. ED gives IV acetaminophen. Which dose is correct?

reference: "For adults weighing 50 kg or more: 1000 mg every 6 hours or 650 mg every 4 hours, with a maximum single dose of OFIRMEV of 1000 mg." "For adults weighing under 50 kg: 15 mg/kg every 6 hours or 12.5 mg/kg every 4 hours, with a maximum single dose of OFIRMEV of 15 mg/kg."

question: A 28-year-old man found unresponsive after suspected fentanyl OD (pinpoint pupils, RR 6, SpO2 82%) was given naloxone 2 mg IN by EMS. He is now awake and protecting his airway, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, with an 18-g peripheral IV in place. He is retching and has vomited twice. No QT-prolonging medications; ECG QTc 410 ms. EMS gives ondansetron for the vomiting. Which order is correct?

reference: Routes: "INTRAVENOUS, INTRAMUSCULAR". "4 mg undiluted administered intravenously in not less than 30 seconds, preferably over 2 to 5 minutes"; alternatively "4 mg undiluted may be administered intramuscularly as a single injection for adults"; chemotherapy prevention uses "three 0.15-mg/kg doses."

question: A 62-year-old man in septic shock remains hypotensive (MAP 58) on norepinephrine 0.4 mcg/kg/min after adequate fluid resuscitation and source control. The ICU team adds vasopressin as a second vasopressor. Which order matches the FDA-labeled starting regimen for septic shock?

choices.B: Vasopressin 0.01 units/min continuous IV infusion, titrated up by 0.005 units/min every 10 to 15 min
choices.C: Vasopressin 0.01 units/min continuous IV infusion, increased by 0.05 units/min every 5 min

reference: "Vasostrict® is indicated to increase blood pressure in adults with vasodilatory shock who remain hypotensive despite fluids and catecholamines." Septic shock starting dose "0.01 units/minute" ... "Titrate up by 0.005 units/minute at 10- to 15-minute intervals until the target blood pressure is reached." ... "There are limited data for doses above 0.1 units/minute for post-cardiotomy shock and 0.07 units/minute for septic shock."

question: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with hematemesis (Hgb 6.8 from 11). He is resuscitated and urgent EGD reveals actively bleeding esophageal varices. The GI team is selecting a management plan. Which is correct?

choices.A: Octreotide infusion + ceftriaxone + endoscopic band ligation
choices.D: Pantoprazole infusion + ceftriaxone + endoscopic band ligation

reference: "Variceal band ligation is recommended as the preferred endoscopic method" (level 1a, grade A). "Vasoconstrictors such as terlipressin or somatostatin are recommended and should be started as soon variceal bleeding is suspected and continued until haemostasis is achieved or for up to 5 days. Octreotide (unlicensed) is suggested if terlipressin or somatostatin are unavailable" (level 1a, grade A). "Antibiotics are recommended for all patients with suspected or confirmed variceal bleeding" (level 1a, grade A).

question: A 62-year-old man presents with 12 hr of epigastric pain. CT shows a small volume of free air with a contained duodenal perforation and no free fluid. He is afebrile, HR 82, BP 128/76, with focal epigastric tenderness and no generalized peritonitis. A water-soluble contrast study shows no extravasation, confirming the perforation has sealed. Surgery is consulted at the bedside, agrees with non-operative management, admits him to the surgical service, and remains ready to operate. He is kept nil by mouth with nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and serial abdominal examinations, and is started on IV pantoprazole 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hr infusion. Which additional therapy does the regimen require?

choices.D: Pantoprazole IV + repeat CT abdomen in 6 hr

reference: "Non-operative management (NOM) could be considered in extremely selected cases where perforation has sealed as confirmed on water-soluble contrast study." NOM "encompasses nil by mouth; intravenous hydration; decompression via nasogastric tube; anti-secretory and PPI therapy; intravenous antibiotics; and follow-up endoscopy at 4–6 weeks." Surgery is recommended for "significant pneumoperitoneum or extraluminal contrast extravasation or signs of peritonitis" and "as soon as possible ... especially in patients with delayed presentation and patients older than 70 years old."

question: A 78-year-old woman with chronic constipation presents for follow-up. Rectal exam shows an empty vault with no impaction; the abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no obstruction on exam or history. She still has only 2 hard bowel movements per week despite 3 months of PEG 3350 17 g daily, and a prior 4-week trial of senna was ineffective. She swallows oral medication without difficulty. The PCP adds a stimulant laxative. Which order is correct?

choices.D: Bisacodyl 10 mg PR + PO daily × 5 d

reference: "take 1 to 3 tablets in a single daily dose" with "a glass of water" (bisacodyl delayed-release tablets, "Bisacodyl USP, 5 mg"); "ask a doctor before use if you have stomach pain, nausea or vomiting"; "stop use and ask a doctor if you need to use a laxative for more than 1 week."

question: A 68-year-old man on hospital day 3 has watery diarrhea Q1h. He is afebrile (T 36.9), WBC 7.2, and the stools are non-bloody. C. difficile toxin EIA and PCR are both negative and stool cultures show no Salmonella, Shigella or Campylobacter; the picture is consistent with non-infectious post-antibiotic osmotic diarrhea. The abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds and no distension. Team gives loperamide for symptomatic control. Which regimen is correct?

choices.A: Loperamide 4 mg PO PRN up to 16 mg/day
choices.C: Loperamide 4 mg PO once, then 2 mg after each unformed stool, max 16 mg/day

reference: "The recommended initial dose is 4mg (two capsules) followed by 2 mg (one capsule) after each unformed stool. Daily dose should not exceed 16mg (eight capsules)." ... IMODIUM should not be used as primary therapy "in patients with acute dysentery, which is characterized by blood in stools and high fever", "in patients with bacterial enterocolitis caused by invasive organisms including Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter", or "in patients with pseudomembranous colitis associated with the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics."

question: An 82-year-old man with no baseline cognitive impairment (no dementia, no parkinsonism, no visual hallucinations at baseline) is hospitalized for a UTI and develops hyperactive delirium with agitation, pulling at lines and striking staff. The infection is being treated and non-pharmacologic measures have failed; he is a danger to himself and staff. ECG shows QTc 420 ms; K and Mg are normal; he is on no other QT-prolonging drug. Team gives haloperidol. Which order is correct?

reference: "HALOPERIDOL INJECTION IS NOT APPROVED FOR INTRAVENOUS ADMINISTRATION." Intravenous use carries heightened risk of QT prolongation and Torsades de Pointes; the approved route is intramuscular only. Initial parenteral doses of "2–5 mg intramuscularly for moderately to very severe symptoms"; debilitated and geriatric patients "require lower doses and more gradual dosage adjustments." Boxed warning: "Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death."

question: A healthy 4-month-old infant with no personal history of intussusception, no severe combined immunodeficiency, and no prior hypersensitivity reaction presents for scheduled vaccines. He received his first RotaTeq dose at 2 months of age and tolerated it. He is afebrile and well. Pediatrics gives the second dose of the rotavirus series. Which order is correct?

reference: "Administer orally as a series of 3 doses starting at 6 to 12 weeks of age, with the subsequent doses administered at 4 to 10 week intervals. The third dose should not be given after 32 weeks of age." Each dose consists of "2 mL." Contraindications: "History of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease (SCID)"; "History of intussusception"; "A demonstrated history of hypersensitivity to the vaccine or any component of the vaccine."

question: A 44-year-old woman with no thymus disorder (no thymoma, no myasthenia gravis, no thymectomy), immunocompetent, not pregnant and not breastfeeding, with no history of acute hypersensitivity to eggs, egg products or gelatin, plans travel to Amazonian Brazil. Travel medicine gives yellow fever vaccine. Which order is correct?

reference: "a single subcutaneous injection of 0.5 mL of reconstituted vaccine"; "YF-VAX is indicated for active immunization for the prevention of yellow fever in persons 9 months of age and older." Contraindicated with "a history of acute hypersensitivity to eggs or egg products due to a risk of anaphylaxis" and with severe immunosuppression including "thymic disease"; "Thymic disorders associated with abnormal immune cell function (e.g., myasthenia gravis, thymoma) may be an independent risk factor."

question: A 28-year-old healthcare worker with no eczema or atopic dermatitis (none currently and none at any time in the past), no other exfoliative skin condition, no immunosuppression, no known cardiac disease or multiple cardiac risk factors, and not pregnant, is enrolled in a first-responder pre-exposure program. She has no household contacts with eczematous conditions, immunosuppression, or pregnancy. Occupational health administers ACAM2000 by scarification at a single deltoid site with a bifurcated needle. Which technique is correct?

reference: "Rapidly make 15 jabs of the needle perpendicular to the skin through the vaccine droplet to puncture the skin, within a diameter of about 5 mm." (The same 15-jab procedure applies to primary vaccination and revaccination.)

question: A 34-year-old newly diagnosed HIV+ man is HLA-B*57:01 NEGATIVE on pre-treatment screening, has no prior exposure to abacavir and no prior hypersensitivity to abacavir, dolutegravir or lamivudine. HBsAg negative, eGFR 105 mL/min, normal hepatic function with no cirrhosis or hepatic impairment, no cardiovascular disease, not taking dofetilide, HIV RNA 48,000 copies/mL, and no transmitted resistance on genotype. ID initiates abacavir/lamivudine/dolutegravir (Triumeq). Which order is correct?

choices.A: Triumeq 1 tab PO daily with allergy pre-medication
choices.C: Triumeq half-dose for 2 weeks then titrate

reference: "The recommended dosage regimen of TRIUMEQ in adults is one tablet once daily orally with or without food." "TRIUMEQ and TRIUMEQ PD are contraindicated in patients: who have the HLA-B*5701 allele; with prior hypersensitivity reaction to abacavir, dolutegravir, or lamivudine; receiving dofetilide ...; with moderate or severe hepatic impairment." "Screen for the HLA-B*5701 allele prior to initiating therapy with TRIUMEQ or TRIUMEQ PD."

question: A 34-year-old woman with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) refractory to at least one prior systemic therapy is not pregnant (negative pregnancy test within 1 week of starting), uses two reliable forms of contraception, and is not breastfeeding. She is not taking gemfibrozil. Baseline fasting triglycerides and TSH are normal and she has no known hypersensitivity to retinoids. Oncology initiates bexarotene. Which starting dose is correct?

reference: "The recommended initial dose of TARGRETIN is 300 mg/m2/day" taken "as a single oral daily dose with a meal." "The 300 mg/m2/day dose level of TARGRETIN may be adjusted to 200 mg/m2/day then to 100 mg/m2/day, or temporarily suspended, if necessitated by toxicity." "TARGRETIN must not be administered to a pregnant woman." "Concomitant administration of TARGRETIN and gemfibrozil is not recommended."

question: A 32-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO Group 1; she does not have idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) has been on ambrisentan 10 mg PO daily for 6 months. She is not pregnant: she is enrolled in the Letairis REMS with a documented negative pregnancy test this month and uses two acceptable forms of contraception. She has tolerated the drug well, with normal LFTs, no peripheral edema, and an improved 6-minute walk distance. PH specialist continues ambrisentan unchanged. Which ambrisentan regimen is appropriate?

choices.C: 5 mg PO daily + monthly pregnancy testing

reference: "Initiate treatment at 5 mg once daily... At 4-week intervals, either the dose of Letairis or tadalafil can be increased, as needed and tolerated, to Letairis 10 mg"; "Letairis is contraindicated in females who are pregnant"; "Letairis is contraindicated in patients with Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF), including IPF patients with pulmonary hypertension (WHO Group 3)"

question: A 28-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension has been on macitentan 10 mg PO daily for 4 months. She is not pregnant: she is enrolled in the Opsumit REMS with a documented negative pregnancy test this month and uses two acceptable forms of contraception. She has no history of hypersensitivity to macitentan, and her hemoglobin and LFTs are normal. Specialist continues macitentan. Which regimen is appropriate?

reference: "The recommended dosage of OPSUMIT is 10 mg once daily for oral administration."; "Doses higher than 10 mg once daily have not been studied in patients with PAH and are not recommended."; "OPSUMIT is contraindicated in females who are pregnant."

question: A 34-year-old woman with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) that persists after pulmonary endarterectomy has been titrated over 10 weeks to riociguat 2.5 mg PO TID. She is not pregnant: she has a documented negative monthly pregnancy test, is enrolled in the Adempas REMS, and uses two acceptable forms of contraception. She takes no nitrate or nitric oxide donor, no PDE-5 inhibitor (specific or nonspecific), and no other soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, and she does not have pulmonary hypertension associated with idiopathic interstitial pneumonia. Systolic BP is 118 mmHg and she has no symptoms of hypotension. Specialist continues riociguat. Which regimen is appropriate?

reference: "The dose can be increased to the highest tolerated dosage, up to a maximum of 2.5 mg taken three times a day."; "If systolic blood pressure remains greater than 95 mmHg and the patient has no signs or symptoms of hypotension, up-titrate the dose by 0.5 mg taken three times a day."; "If at any time, the patient has symptoms of hypotension, decrease the dosage by 0.5 mg taken three times a day."; "Use of Adempas is contraindicated in patients who are pregnant"

question: A 51-year-old man with Child-Pugh B cirrhosis has had two episodes of overt hepatic encephalopathy in the past 6 months despite adherent lactulose therapy. He has no drug allergies and, specifically, no history of hypersensitivity to rifampin, rifabutin, rifapentine or any other rifamycin, and no prior exposure to rifaximin. GI starts rifaximin for reduction in the risk of overt HE recurrence. Which regimen is appropriate?

reference: "The recommended dosage of XIFAXAN is 550 mg taken orally two times a day." (hepatic encephalopathy); "The recommended dosage of XIFAXAN is 200 mg taken orally three times a day for 3 days." (travelers' diarrhea); "contraindicated in patients with a hypersensitivity to rifaximin, any of the rifamycin antimicrobial agents, or any of the components in XIFAXAN"

question: A 66-year-old man is 6 months post-MI and takes aspirin 81 mg daily. He has never had a stroke, a TIA or an intracranial hemorrhage, has no active pathological bleeding and no history of peptic ulcer disease, and has normal renal and hepatic function. Cardiology adds vorapaxar (Zontivity) for reduction of thrombotic cardiovascular events. Which regimen is appropriate?

choices.C: 2.08 mg PO daily × 12 mo then stop

reference: "Take one tablet of ZONTIVITY 2.08 mg orally once daily, with or without food."; "Use ZONTIVITY with aspirin and/or clopidogrel according to their indications or standard of care."; "ZONTIVITY is contraindicated in patients with a history of stroke, TIA, or ICH because of an increased risk of ICH in this population."; "ZONTIVITY is contraindicated in patients with active pathological bleeding such as ICH or peptic ulcer."

question: A 71-year-old man has just undergone PCI for NSTEMI. He has no history of intracranial hemorrhage, stroke or TIA, no active pathological bleeding, no hypersensitivity to ticagrelor, and normal hepatic function. He is not at high bleeding risk and the plan is 12 months of dual antiplatelet therapy. He has received a 180 mg ticagrelor loading dose and is on aspirin 81 mg daily. Cardiology continues ticagrelor. Which maintenance regimen is appropriate for the coming year?

choices.A: 90 mg PO BID × 6 mo then reassess

reference: "Initiate treatment with 180 mg oral loading dose of BRILINTA. Then administer 90 mg twice daily during the first year."; "After one year, administer 60 mg twice daily."; "Use BRILINTA with a daily maintenance dose of aspirin of 75-100 mg."; "BRILINTA is contraindicated in patients with a history of intracranial hemorrhage."

question: A 71-year-old man with metastatic (Stage D2) prostate cancer underwent bilateral orchiectomy yesterday. He has no cirrhosis and normal baseline hepatic enzymes, no severe respiratory insufficiency or interstitial lung disease, and no hypersensitivity to nilutamide. Oncology initiates nilutamide today as combined androgen blockade with the orchiectomy. Which nilutamide regimen is appropriate?

choices.A: 100 mg PO daily x 30 d -> 200 mg PO daily
choices.B: 150 mg PO daily x 30 d -> 300 mg PO daily
choices.C: 300 mg PO daily x 30 d -> 150 mg PO daily

reference: "The recommended dosage is 300 mg once a day for 30 days, followed thereafter by 150 mg once a day."; "Nilutamide Tablets are indicated for use in combination with surgical castration for the treatment of metastatic prostate cancer (Stage D2)."; "For maximum benefit, treatment with Nilutamide Tablets must begin on the same day as or on the day after surgical castration."; Nilutamide Tablets are contraindicated in patients with "Severe hepatic impairment (baseline hepatic enzymes should be evaluated prior to treatment)", "Severe respiratory insufficiency", and "Hypersensitivity to nilutamide or any component of this preparation".

question: A 34-year-old healthcare worker is offered vaccinia vaccine as first-responder pre-exposure prophylaxis. His wife completed chemotherapy for lymphoma 2 years ago, has been in sustained remission off all therapy since, and has a normal ANC of 4,200/µL. No one in the household is pregnant, under 1 year of age, immunocompromised, or affected by eczema or another exfoliative skin condition. He himself is immunocompetent, has no eczema, and has no known cardiac disease or cardiac risk factors. Occupational health gives ACAM2000. Which administration is correct?

reference: "Rapidly make 15 jabs of the needle perpendicular to the skin through the vaccine droplet"; "Do not administer ACAM2000 to individuals with severe immunodeficiency."

question: A 4-year-old boy with no chronic medical conditions attends an October vaccination visit. He has no asthma and no episode of wheezing in the past 12 months, is not immunocompromised, has no immunocompromised household contact requiring a protected environment, receives no aspirin or aspirin-containing therapy, and has had no severe allergic reaction to egg or to any previous influenza vaccine. He has a normal anatomic airway with no CSF leak and no cochlear implant, and has taken no influenza antiviral. He received two doses of influenza vaccine in a prior season. He is offered LAIV (FluMist) intranasally. Which administration is correct?

reference: "A single dose is 0.2 mL" administered as "0.1 mL per nostril"; children 2–8 years receive "1 or 2 doses, 0.2 mL each" depending on vaccination history; "Do not administer FluMist to persons who have had a severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any component of the vaccine including egg protein, or after a previous dose of any influenza vaccine."; "Do not administer FluMist to children and adolescents through 17 years of age who are receiving aspirin therapy or aspirin-containing therapy."

question: A 44-year-old man with HIV is starting antiretroviral therapy. He has no cirrhosis and normal hepatic function (no Child-Pugh class B or C impairment), is hepatitis B and hepatitis C negative, drinks no alcohol, and has a CD4 count of 180 cells/mm3. This is initial treatment of established HIV infection, not occupational or non-occupational post-exposure prophylaxis. ID initiates nevirapine as part of an NNRTI-based regimen with two nucleoside analogues. Which nevirapine regimen is appropriate?

choices.B: 200 mg PO daily indefinitely (no dose escalation)
choices.C: 100 mg PO daily × 14 d → 200 mg BID

reference: "The recommended dose for nevirapine is one 200 mg tablet daily for the first 14 days" "followed by one 200 mg tablet twice daily, in combination with other antiretroviral agents"; contraindicated in "Patients with moderate or severe (Child-Pugh Class B or C, respectively) hepatic impairment" and for "Use as part of occupational and non-occupational post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimens"

question: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is DPYD wild-type on pharmacogenomic testing, with no dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency. She has no history of severe hypersensitivity to fluorouracil or capecitabine, her creatinine clearance is 92 mL/min, and she takes no warfarin, phenytoin or allopurinol. Oncology plans single-agent capecitabine on a 21-day cycle. Which regimen is appropriate?

choices.D: 1250 mg/m² PO BID D1-14 per label

reference: "The recommended dosage of XELODA is 1,000 mg/m2 or 1,250 mg/m2 orally twice daily for the first 14 days of a 21-day cycle until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity."; "XELODA is contraindicated in patients with history of severe hypersensitivity reaction to fluorouracil or capecitabine"

question: A 34-year-old woman with bipolar II depression is maintained on lamotrigine 200 mg PO daily. She takes no monoamine oxidase inhibitor and no serotonergic antidepressant, and has taken neither within the past 14 days. She develops a complicated MRSA skin and skin-structure infection - extensive cellulitis with an abscess that has been drained. She tolerates oral intake, has no intravenous access, and is being managed as an outpatient. ID initiates linezolid. Which regimen is appropriate?

choices.A: Linezolid 1200 mg PO once daily + continue lamotrigine
choices.B: Linezolid 400 mg PO BID + continue lamotrigine
choices.C: Linezolid 600 mg PO BID + continue lamotrigine
choices.D: Linezolid 600 mg PO daily + continue lamotrigine

reference: "ZYVOX is indicated for the treatment of uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible isolates only) or Streptococcus pyogenes"; "ZYVOX is indicated for the treatment of complicated skin and skin structure infections, including diabetic foot infections, without concomitant osteomyelitis, caused by Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible and -resistant isolates), Streptococcus pyogenes, or Streptococcus agalactiae."; complicated skin and skin structure infections, adults: 600 mg intravenously or orally every 12 hours for 14 to 28 days; uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections, adults: 400 mg orally every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days; "Linezolid should not be used in patients taking any medicinal product which inhibits monoamine oxidases A or B (e.g., phenelzine, isocarboxazid) or within two weeks of taking any such medicinal product."

question: A 58-year-old man with invasive aspergillosis has been on voriconazole 200 mg PO BID for 3 weeks with clinical and radiographic improvement. His epilepsy is well controlled on levetiracetam 1000 mg PO BID.

choices.A: Voriconazole 400 mg BID + levetiracetam 1000 mg BID
choices.B: Voriconazole 800 mg loading dose + levetiracetam 1000 mg BID
choices.C: Voriconazole 600 mg BID + levetiracetam 1000 mg BID
choices.D: Voriconazole 200 mg BID + levetiracetam 1000 mg BID

reference: Maintenance Dose: 200 mg every 12 hours ... If the patient's response is inadequate, the oral maintenance dose ... may be increased from 200 mg ... every 12 hours to 300 mg ... every 12 hours.

question: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease on carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 four times daily and selegiline 5 mg PO BID has end-of-dose wearing off. Neurology adds entacapone.

choices.A: Selegiline 5 mg BID + entacapone 200 mg with each levodopa dose
choices.B: Selegiline 10 mg once daily at bedtime + entacapone 200 mg with each levodopa dose
choices.C: Selegiline 2.5 mg BID + entacapone 200 mg with each levodopa dose
choices.D: Selegiline 5 mg daily + entacapone 100 mg with each levodopa dose

reference: one 200 mg tablet administered concomitantly with each levodopa and carbidopa dose ... to a maximum of 8 times daily ... Entacapone can be taken concomitantly with a selective MAO-B inhibitor (e.g., selegiline).

question: A 51-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on lithium 900 mg PO daily (trough 0.9 mEq/L) develops new-onset heart failure with EF 30%. She is NYHA class II, clinically euvolemic, and is not taking a diuretic. Cardiology plans to start a beta-blocker.

reference: COREG label: "The recommended starting dose of COREG is 3.125 mg twice daily for 2 weeks." ... "Prior to initiation of COREG, it is recommended that fluid retention be minimized." Lithium carbonate label: "Maintenance Treatment for Bipolar I Disorder (patients 7 years and older): Titrate to serum lithium concentrations 0.8 to 1 mEq/L" ... "Diuretic-induced sodium loss may reduce lithium clearance and increase serum lithium concentrations."

question: A 58-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on lithium 1200 mg PO daily (trough 0.9 mEq/L, stable for 2 years) is newly diagnosed with essential hypertension at 156/96 mmHg. Renal function is normal. Her PCP starts metoprolol succinate 50 mg PO daily.

choices.A: Lithium 900 mg + metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily
choices.B: Lithium 900 mg + metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily
choices.C: Lithium 1200 mg + metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily

reference: "Maintenance Treatment for Bipolar I Disorder (patients 7 years and older): Titrate to serum lithium concentrations 0.8 to 1 mEq/L"; "Diuretic-induced sodium loss may reduce lithium clearance and increase serum lithium concentrations." The Drug Interactions section (7.1) names diuretics, NSAIDs, renin-angiotensin system antagonists, serotonergic drugs, nitroimidazole antibiotics, acetazolamide/urea/xanthine preparations/alkalinizing agents, methyldopa, phenytoin and carbamazepine, iodide preparations, calcium channel blocking agents, atypical and typical antipsychotic drugs, SGLT2 inhibitors, and neuromuscular blocking agents; beta-adrenergic blockers do not appear.

question: A 62-year-old man with bipolar disorder maintained on divalproex sodium ER 1500 mg PO daily (valproate trough 92 mcg/mL) develops new hypertension at 152/94 mmHg with microalbuminuria. He takes no lithium. PCP starts lisinopril 20 mg PO daily.

choices.A: Divalproex ER 1000 mg + lisinopril 20 mg daily
choices.B: Divalproex ER 1000 mg + lisinopril 10 mg daily
choices.C: Divalproex ER 1500 mg + lisinopril 20 mg + losartan 50 mg daily
choices.D: Divalproex ER 1500 mg + lisinopril 20 mg daily

reference: Lisinopril monotherapy is an effective treatment of hypertension in once-daily doses of 10 mg to 80 mg. ... [losartan label:] In general, avoid combined use of RAS inhibitors. ... Dual blockade of the RAS ... is associated with increased risks of hypotension, syncope, hyperkalemia, and changes in renal function (including acute renal failure) compared to monotherapy.

question: A 68-year-old man on alfuzosin 10 mg XL PO daily for BPH develops invasive candidiasis with candidemia. He has no hepatic impairment. ID initiates micafungin 100 mg IV daily.
